slides.title: 95% coverage, still broken in production
slides.tldr: Coverage tells you which lines ran, not whether they are right. If most tests sit on easy code, the bugs pile up in the risky spots.

blocks.title: Locks on the house
blocks.body: A family keeps its jewelry in a safe and a broom on the porch. Sensible people put a strong lock on the safe, not on the broom. But one person decides "everything gets the same lock", fits 400 boxes with locks, and leaves the safe with an old rusty one. Tests work the same way: put the most of them where a break hurts most. Piling tests onto easy code just to raise coverage doesn't help.

blocks.caption: Coverage is 95%, yet tests and bugs are spread in exactly opposite ways, and the last column moves the effort

rows.tip: There is nothing in this code to break. It has the most lines, though, so it inflates the coverage number. Keep a few and move the effort.
Thresholds, percentages and conditions are tangled together here, and money is directly involved. Cheap unit tests on both sides of every threshold.
This is where you join an outside service. Nobody wrote tests because it looked hard to mock. Test paid, failed and duplicate deliveries.
One migration mistake puts the whole database at risk. Run each one on old-shaped, messy data.

blocks.body: Coverage tells you which lines ran, not which lines are safe.

aside.title: Green CI, wrong price
aside.body: One team blocked every merge that dropped coverage below 90%. Everyone kept the number up by adding tests to easy classes. Meanwhile, a `>` in the discount threshold should have been `>=`. For a week, orders sitting exactly on the threshold got no discount, and no test caught it.

items.meaning: The percentage of code lines that ran at least once during the tests. It doesn't say whether they ran correctly.
Something that used to work and broke after a new change.

check.q: Coverage is 95%, yet a bug remains in the price calculation. What could the coverage number not tell you?
check.a: The pricing lines may have run once, but nobody checked whether the threshold, the percentage or the condition is right. The number counts "ran", not "correct".

slides.title: Test by risk: the three layers of the pyramid
slides.tldr: Lots of fast unit tests, some integration tests, a few end-to-end ones. Risk decides where to add more: the bigger the damage and the likelier the break, the more tests.

blocks.body: There are three kinds of tests. A **unit test** checks one small piece in isolation, with no database or network, so it runs in milliseconds. An **integration test** runs several pieces together, with a real database or real HTTP. An **end-to-end (E2E) test** walks the whole journey from the browser to the database. The higher you go, the closer to reality the test gets, but the slower and more brittle it becomes (brittle: it breaks for small, unrelated reasons).

blocks.caption: The pyramid: many at the bottom, few at the top

layers.label: End-to-end
layers.sub: A few: only the main journeys
layers.tip: For example, one path from login to placing an order. Slow (seconds to minutes), and even a small UI change can break it.

layers.label: Integration
layers.tip: The seams: queries, config, controllers. This is where you catch what unit tests can't.

layers.label: Unit
layers.sub: Many: calculations and rules, in milliseconds
layers.tip: Price calculation, date rules, threshold values. They are cheap and fast, so check every value near a boundary here.

blocks.title: Where to add tests first
items: Big damage: money, data loss, security (payments, discounts, permissions)
Changes often: a rule everyone keeps touching
Complex: many conditions, or values close to a boundary
Seams (where two parts join): queries, config, outside APIs

blocks.body: Write tests in proportion to the risk, not in proportion to the lines of code.

aside.body: The higher the layer, the more real but the slower. So: few on top, many at the bottom.
Test everything end to end and the suite takes an hour, breaks all the time, and nobody runs it. Write only unit tests and you miss mistakes at the seams (a wrong query, a wrong config).

use: Logic-heavy code (prices, rules, calculations): many unit tests, a few integration tests.
avoid: Thin glue with little logic, like plain CRUD: unit tests there mostly test mocks, so lean on integration tests.

check.q: You want to check 10 boundary values in the price calculation. Which layer do you write them in, and why?
check.a: The unit layer: it runs in milliseconds and needs no database, so dozens of values are cheap to check. The same job in E2E would be slow and brittle.

slides.title: PHPUnit: unit tests and KernelTestCase
slides.tldr: For pure calculations, use a plain TestCase with a DataProvider. For database queries or wiring between services, use KernelTestCase with the real container and database.

blocks.body: The pricing rule is an ordinary class, so you can test it without any framework. Put the values near the boundary in a `DataProvider`, so one test function runs dozens of cases. Where you need the container (the box that holds all your services) and a database, such as a Doctrine query, use `KernelTestCase`. The boundary cases matter most: if the code wrongly says `>` where the rule says "10,000 cents ($100) or more", an order of exactly 10,000 gets no discount. The case at 10,000 below fails with `Failed asserting that 0 is identical to 1000`; tests at 5,000 and 20,000 would pass either way.

marks.tip: In PHPUnit 10+ the DataProvider is an attribute. The provider method must be static.
9_999 and 10_000: exactly either side of the threshold. Most bugs hide right there (> versus >=).
Write readable case names. When a case fails, PHPUnit shows that name, which makes the failure easy to understand.
bootKernel() starts the real container and Doctrine in the test environment.
self::getContainer() is the special test container, which also gives you access to private services.
Three orders of three kinds: an old pending one (should be found), a new pending one, an old paid one. The two that must not be found are checked here too.

items.desc: Run the migrations on the test database

items: dama/doctrine-test-bundle wraps each test in a transaction and rolls it back at the end, so data stays clean and tests run fast.
The test database should match production (PostgreSQL), not SQLite. More on that in the next topic.

items.label: Integration tests against a real database

check.q: In the price test, why check both the value one cent below the threshold and the value exactly on it?
check.a: Most calculation bugs live at the boundary: mixing up `>` and `>=`. Without values on both sides of the threshold, the test won't catch that mistake.

slides.title: WebTestCase: does the HTTP path work?
slides.tldr: Use WebTestCase to send real HTTP requests into your app: routing, validation, serialization and security in one test. Keep browser E2E tests for the main journeys only.

blocks.body: HTTP is the best place to test what the client actually sees. The `WebTestCase` client sends requests into your app without a browser, so it's fast, yet routing, validation, the serializer and security are all the real thing. The table below shows how the three layers differ.

marks.tip: createClient() boots a fresh kernel for every test. You start from a known state, with no leftovers from earlier tests.
Check the body, not just the status. Getting a 422 isn't enough: verify which error was reported.

blocks.caption: The three kinds of tests in Symfony

rows.tip: Panther drives a real browser. Playwright is a separate tool, but many people use it for this.
The more parts a test touches, the more realistic it is, and the slower and more brittle.
This is why the pyramid is widest at the bottom.
Each layer catches a different kind of mistake, so none replaces another.

blocks.body: At the HTTP layer, test exactly what the client sees: status, headers and body.

items: Keep E2E tests to a handful: login, placing an order, payment. Everything else goes in the lower layers.
In WebTestCase, put a MockHttpClient in the test environment for outside APIs, or calls will hit the real service.
Cart ids like 'empty-cart' are fixtures: create them in the test (or load fixtures) so each test sets up exactly the data it needs.

check.q: You send an empty cart to the checkout API. Why isn't `assertResponseStatusCodeSame(422)` alone enough?
check.a: A 422 can come back for any reason. Checking that the body contains violations shows why it failed, and catches a test that passes for the wrong reason.

slides.title: The trap: mock-heavy tests and coverage targets
slides.tldr: A test that only checks "was the method called" passes even with the wrong price. Verify the outcome, use fakes, and treat coverage as a signal, not a goal.

blocks.body: In the test below, everything is mocked. It only checks that `save()` was called once. But `save()` is called even when the price is wrong, so the test stays green on broken code. And it breaks when you refactor the insides, even though the behavior is right. Both are bad.

marks.tip: This line pins down how the code works inside (which method it calls). Refactor it and the test breaks, even though the code is still correct.
The real question, whether the total is right, is never asked.
A fake is a small real implementation. How it works is not your concern, only whether the result is right.
10,000 - 10% = 9,000. If the price is wrong, the test fails on this line, which is exactly what you want.

blocks.title: How to look at coverage
items: A drop in coverage is a warning sign, but high coverage is no proof of safety
Set a coverage target and people pile useless tests onto easy code
A better question: "If this line broke, would any test fail?"
Infection (mutation testing) plants small bugs in your code on purpose and checks whether the tests catch them. Run it now and then on your most valuable code.
You need a mock when the call itself is the result (for example, sending an email exactly once). Even then, use a fake if you can.
The price of a fake: it can drift from the real thing. Keep one integration test on the real repository (the KernelTestCase slide) so the two stay in step.

use: fake: for simple dependencies like a repository, a clock or an email inbox

check.q: You refactored the internals but the behavior is the same, and a test broke. What is the likely cause?
check.a: The test pinned down the implementation, not the result: which methods get called and how often. If it verified the outcome, the refactor wouldn't break it.

slides.title: Every unit test is green, yet the courier API broke us
slides.tldr: Each kind of test catches a different kind of bug. When the courier API renames a field, unit tests stay green because the mock still returns the old response. That is why you need five kinds.

blocks.title: Hospital check-ups
blocks.body: A doctor never runs just one test on a patient. A blood test finds one kind of illness, an X-ray another, and a treadmill stress test shows whether the heart can take the strain. Passing one doesn't mean you pass the rest. Software is the same: each kind of test catches its own kind of bug and misses the others.

Our shipping code reads the `charge_cents` field from the courier's API. One day the courier quietly renames it to `charge`. Our unit tests still get the old response from a **mock** (a stand-in that returns a canned answer instead of calling the real API), so everything is green, yet in production the delivery charge comes out as zero.

blocks.caption: Five kinds of tests: what each catches and what it misses

rows.tip: Fast, but blind to anything beyond the mock.

cells: Field or type changes in an outside API
rows.tip: Checks that what we expect matches what the other side actually sends.
Runs against the real database or queue, so it catches mistakes at the seams, the places where two parts meet.
Applies a crowd and sees which part runs out of breath first.

cells: Whether behavior is right during failures
rows.tip: Deliberately breaks a dependency to see if the fallback (plan B) and the breaker (a switch that stops calling a sick service) really work.

blocks.body: Each kind of test catches its own kind of bug. One green doesn't mean all green.

aside.title: The silently renamed field
aside.body: An e-commerce team's courier service once switched to a new version and renamed a field. Every test the team had still passed. For seven hours orders went out with a delivery charge of 0, because the code had a `?? 0` fallback. Nobody realized that anything had broken.

check.q: A field in the courier API got renamed. Which kind of test would have caught it, and why didn't the unit test?
check.a: A contract test would have, because it compares our expectation (a schema) with the real response. In a unit test the mock returns the old response, so the change never shows up.

slides.title: Contract tests: checking the deal between two sides
slides.tldr: Write down what you expect from an outside API in a schema file. Your tests build their mock from that file, and a nightly run checks the real sandbox's response against the same schema.

blocks.body: Two sides keep a written contract: "the response will contain an integer called `charge_cents`." A **contract test** checks that contract from both directions. On our side: does our code read it as promised? On the other side: does the real API still keep the promise? Here we are the consumer (the one who uses the API) and the courier is the provider (the one who supplies it).

blocks.caption: The contract file binds both sides

nodes.label: Our app
nodes.tip: Our tests build their mock from exactly this contract, so the mock never returns an imagined response.

nodes.label: Contract (schema)
nodes.tip: Writes down what we expect: which fields, what types. It lives in the repository.

nodes.label: Courier sandbox
nodes.tip: The courier's test environment. No real money or real deliveries are involved.

edges.label: We write down what we expect
The mock in our tests is built from this contract
The nightly test checks the real response against the contract
If they don't match, the test fails and we know early

marks.tip: A separate group, because it is slow and depends on an outside network. Running it on every commit would make CI brittle.
The real sandbox, not production. The token comes from an environment variable, not from the code.
On failure, getErrors() says exactly which field didn't match, so you don't have to guess.
This example file lives next to the schema. If the schema changes, the example must change too, or the nightly test catches it.

items.meaning: The side that calls someone else's API and depends on its response.
The side that supplies the API. If it changes a field, the consumer breaks.

items: If you give your own API to others, do the reverse too: check the consumers' expectations (Pact or OpenAPI) in your CI.
A sandbox doesn't always behave like production. So treat this test as a signal, not proof; when it fails, investigate.

check.q: Why is the mock response in the unit test taken from the contract's example file instead of JSON you wrote yourself?
check.a: A mock you write yourself is imagination, and nobody knows whether it matches reality. If the contract example is checked against the real response every night, the mock stays tied to reality.

slides.title: The contract file, and what a rename looks like
slides.tldr: Mark the fields you read as required in the schema. When the courier renames one, the nightly run fails and names it, instead of orders shipping at 0. Cost: you hear a day late.

blocks.body: The contract is a short **JSON Schema** file: a description of what a JSON response must look like. It marks `charge_cents` as **required** and a whole number. That one word is what stops the story's `?? 0` from hiding the rename, because a missing field is now a failure, not a zero. The example file beside it, `{"charge_cents": 1200, "currency": "USD"}`, is what the unit test uses (1,200 cents is $12.00).

marks.tip: Without this line a missing field passes validation silently, and the code's fallback turns it into a zero charge.
List only the fields we actually read. Extra fields the courier adds later are allowed, so harmless additions don't fail the run.

blocks.file: nightly run, the morning after the rename
blocks.code:
1) CourierContractTest::testSandboxResponseMatchesOurSchema
[{"property":"charge_cents","message":"The property charge_cents is required"}]

marks.tip: The failure names the exact field. We learn the same morning, not after seven hours of zero charges.

blocks.title: When the nightly run goes red
items: Read the field name in the message: the courier changed `charge_cents`.
Change the schema and the example file to the new name, `charge`.
The unit test now fails, because `CourierRateProvider` still reads the old name.
Fix the provider until the unit test and the nightly run are both green.

use: You depend on an outside API you don't control, and a wrong field would cost money.
avoid: As your only safety net: it fires up to a day late, and a sandbox can differ from production. Keep a production alert on charges of 0 too.

items: Don't put every field in `required`: list only what the code reads, or the courier adding a field breaks your build for nothing.

check.q: Why does marking `charge_cents` as required matter after the courier renames it?
check.a: Without it, a missing field passes validation and the code's `?? 0` quietly makes the charge zero. With it, the nightly run fails and names the field.

slides.title: Integration tests: a real database, not a mock
slides.tldr: Run PostgreSQL in tests, just like production. SQLite or a mock hides the real behavior of unique indexes, JSONB, FOR UPDATE and migrations.

blocks.body: To make tests fast, many teams use SQLite or an in-memory database. But production runs PostgreSQL, and the differences sit exactly where the bugs hide. The test below checks a rule that lives in PostgreSQL's own index: the same email in a different letter case must be refused. Whether that index is right, only a real PostgreSQL run can show.

blocks.caption: Mistakes only a real database catches

cells: Blocks the same email in different letter case
rows.tip: The code assumes emails are unique. Whether the index really is case-insensitive, only the real database knows.
This is the whole basis of a pessimistic lock. Test on SQLite and you will never learn whether the lock works.
Mistakes in queries on JSON fields, and use of their indexes, can only be tested here.
The SQL you wrote in the migration will run on the production database, so test it there.

blocks.code:
services:
  database_test:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: app_test
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test_only
    ports: ['5433:5432']
    tmpfs: ['/var/lib/postgresql/data']   # in memory: fast, wiped when stopped

marks.tip: Exactly the same major version as production. Test on 15 and run on 16, and even small differences are dangerous.
The database files live in RAM, so tests are much faster. This data isn't meant to be kept, so that's fine.
The test expects one specific exception. If it doesn't come, the unique index wasn't set up properly.

items: In .env.test, set DATABASE_URL to postgresql://app:test_only@127.0.0.1:5433/app_test?serverVersion=16. It is for tests only, not a real password.
Run the same compose.test.yaml in CI, so your machine and CI use the same database.
The same goes for RabbitMQ or Redis: if you rely on a dependency's behavior, keep the real one in your tests.
The price: slower than a unit test, and it needs Docker. For pure calculations keep the unit test; use integration tests for seams like queries, indexes, locks and migrations.

check.q: Tests are green on SQLite, but duplicate emails get into production PostgreSQL. What is the likely cause?
check.a: On SQLite the unique index on LOWER(email) behaves differently, or isn't created at all. PostgreSQL's real behavior only shows up when you run against real PostgreSQL.

slides.title: Load tests: create a crowd with k6
slides.tldr: In a k6 script, describe how the crowd ramps up and set thresholds (p95 < 500ms, failures < 1%). When a threshold is crossed the test fails by itself, so you can put it in CI.

blocks.body: Think of the hospital treadmill: the heart is fine at rest, but what happens when you run? A load test creates an artificial crowd (**virtual users**) and shows where slowness or failures begin. 50 virtual users who each pause a second between clicks send about 50 requests a second, like 50 people each tapping refresh once a second. A k6 script is plain JavaScript, so it is easy to keep in the repository.

marks.tip: stages raise the crowd step by step, not all at once. That shows at which number the slowness starts.
When a threshold is crossed, k6 exits with a non-zero code, so the test fails in CI. Derive the numbers from your SLO, the speed promise you made to users.
Without sleep, a virtual user fires requests at machine speed. With a 20ms response that is about 50 a second per user, so 50 users become about 2,500 a second instead of about 50.

cells: Does it run fine on a normal day?
rows.tip: The baseline. If you don't pass this first, there is no point in the others.

cells: Raises the crowd until it breaks
The breaking point, and what breaks first
rows.tip: You learn how many you can handle, and how the system fails past that limit: gracefully, or in a heap?

cells: The jolt of a sale or an ad
rows.tip: This tests autoscaling and queue limits. A slowly growing crowd would never expose them.
Slow problems that a 10-minute test will never show.

blocks.body: Run load tests on a staging copy that looks like production: real data volume, real server size.

items.desc: Run the script; exit code is non-zero if a threshold fails

items: Test against an empty database and everything looks fast. Keep production-sized data on staging, or the results lie.
The slowness of the first minute (cold cache) blends into the results. Add a warm-up stage or look at it separately.
Never aim a load test at a third party's API, or at production without warning: to them it looks like an attack.

check.q: The k6 script has no `sleep(1)`. Why does that make the results misleading?
check.a: Each virtual user fires requests without pause, which isn't how real users behave: about 50 a second each instead of about 1. The system breaks with few users, and the "how many users can it handle" number comes out wrong.

slides.title: Chaos tests: break things on purpose to see if the fallback works
slides.tldr: A fallback or breaker that only exists on paper can't be trusted. Inject a 503 or a timeout with MockHttpClient, and create real slowness on staging with Toxiproxy.

blocks.body: Another hospital-style check: what does a bus do when a tire blows out? A **chaos test** deliberately breaks one dependency and checks that the system behaves as expected. Start small: first inject failures in code tests, then on staging (a rehearsal copy of the site) over a real network. The code test fails until the provider handles the failure, and the second code block shows that handling.

blocks.caption: The five steps of a chaos experiment

steps.title: 1. Normal state
steps.body: Measure what healthy looks like: say, checkout success at 99%.
steps.tip: If you don't measure the steady state, you can't tell afterwards whether anything really changed.

steps.title: 2. Write a hypothesis
steps.body: If the courier is down, checkout still succeeds, with just the default charge.
steps.tip: Write down what you expect to happen before the test. If it doesn't match, that is the lesson.

steps.title: 3. Break it small
steps.body: One dependency, a short time, a small share of traffic.
steps.tip: Change only one thing at first, or you can't tell what caused the result.

steps.title: 4. Observe
steps.body: Measure error rate, latency and breaker state.
steps.tip: Keep the dashboard open. Decide beforehand what you would have to see to stop.

steps.title: 5. Fix it
steps.body: If the hypothesis was wrong, file the bug, fix it and run it again.
steps.tip: The real win is the fix, not the discovery. If you don't fix it, the same thing happens next time.

marks.tip: In real life, a 503 makes HttpClient throw a ServerException.
With `error`, MockResponse throws a TransportException when the response is read, just like a real timeout or a dropped connection.
The question the test asks: on failure, does the app crash, or does it gracefully return null?

ExceptionInterface (Symfony Contracts) is the parent of server errors, transport errors and bad JSON. Without this catch, the test above fails with a ServerException and checkout would show an error page.
The hypothesis from step 2 in code: checkout carries on with a default charge ($8.00) when the courier is down.

items.desc: Put a proxy in front of the courier; point the app's courier URL at port 18080

items.cmd: toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=3000 courier
items.desc: Add 3 seconds to every response. With a 2 second timeout every call should time out and the breaker should open
Remove the toxic when the experiment is over

items: A default is a business decision: a flat $8.00 may undercharge a far-away zone. Log and alert whenever the fallback is used.
Don't do chaos in production on day one. Start with unit tests and staging, then a small scope during low traffic.
Never run chaos without a stop switch: decide in advance what you would have to see to halt it immediately.

check.q: Why do you need both `http_code => 503` and `error => ...` in MockResponse?
check.a: They are two different failures: a 503 means the server answered but is unhealthy; an error means a network problem or timeout, with no answer at all. You need to see the code behave correctly in both cases.

slides.title: The bugs that never show up when a test runs alone
slides.tldr: Concurrency, idempotency and migration bugs slip past ordinary tests, because tests run one after another, alone. Yet these are exactly what breaks in production, so they need dedicated tests.

blocks.title: Two brothers at two ATMs
blocks.body: Two brothers share an account with $1,000. At the same moment they walk up to two different ATMs and each tries to withdraw $1,000. Both machines check the balance first ($1,000), and then both hand out the cash. Test either ATM alone and it works perfectly. The mistake only appears when both brothers come together. Code tests usually run "alone" in the same way.

blocks.caption: One item left, two buyers, two orders

actors.label: Buyer Ryan
actors.tip: Placing an order, believing he is the only buyer.

actors.label: Buyer Kevin
actors.tip: Buying the same product at exactly the same moment.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: The stock column says 1. Both of them read it.

messages.label: Read the stock
messages.tip: SELECT stock FROM product WHERE sku = ...

messages.note: Two orders, but there was only one item

blocks.body: A race condition never happens in tests that run one after another.

aside.title: 120 orders too many in a flash sale
aside.body: A sale had 100 phones in stock and sold 220. The team's tests showed stock going down correctly, because they ran with a single buyer, one step at a time. The bug only appeared when thousands of buyers arrived together.

items.meaning: When two tasks run at the same time, the result depends on which one gets there first.
Doing the same thing several times has the same effect as doing it once.

check.q: The stock-reduction test always passes with a single buyer, yet production oversells. What is missing from the test?
check.a: It runs one buyer at a time, in sequence. The situation where two buyers read the stock together, and things go wrong, is never created in the test.

slides.title: 10 buyers at once: writing a concurrency test
slides.tldr: Launch many buyers in separate processes, start them all at the same instant, then check that stock never went negative and exactly one item sold. The next slide shows the bug it catches.

blocks.body: To build a real crowd, launch 10 separate PHP processes at once. Each buys through its own database connection. To make them all start at the same instant, give everyone a start time (`--start-at`). Each process calls `time_sleep_until($startAt)` before it buys, like runners waiting for the starter's whistle. That shared start is called a **barrier**. At the end, check the state of the database, not what each buyer did.

marks.tip: Each process is separate, so each takes a different time to start. If they all wait until this moment, they run off together.
start() doesn't wait, so all 10 processes run almost at once. With run() or mustRun() they would run one after another.
The question isn't "who won" but "is the final state correct": whatever the buggy order of events, these two numbers will catch it.

blocks.body: In a concurrency test, check the final state: stock is never negative, and sales never exceed the items available.

items: This test can't run inside a transaction-wrapped test (DAMA): other processes can't see uncommitted data. Keep a separate suite and TRUNCATE the tables yourself at the start.
Run this test against the old, broken code and check that it fails. If it doesn't, the test itself is weak.

items.meaning: A shared start time everyone waits for, so they all begin together.
A test bundle that wraps each test in a transaction and rolls it back, so every test starts clean.

check.q: Why does the test launch each Process with `start()` and not `mustRun()`?
check.a: `mustRun()` waits for one process to finish, so the buyers arrive one after another and there is no race. `start()` launches them all at almost the same time.

slides.title: Read first, write later oversells: one atomic UPDATE fixes it
slides.tldr: Checking stock in one statement and decrementing in another leaves a gap where other buyers slip in. One UPDATE with `stock > 0` closes it, but only for a single row; bigger rules need a lock.

blocks.body: Run the concurrency test against the usual first draft below and it fails, say with `stock = -3`: four orders went through for one item. The number changes from run to run, but anything except 0 means the test caught the bug. The gap is the line between the SELECT and the UPDATE: the moment both brothers have seen 1,000 on their ATM screens and neither has withdrawn yet.

marks.tip: The check uses a value that is already out of date by the time the write happens.
Nothing re-checks the stock here, so every buyer who passed the check decrements it: stock goes to -3.
The transaction makes the decrement and the order one unit: if the INSERT fails, the decrement is rolled back too.
Reading and writing in one SQL statement: the stock > 0 check and the decrement happen together, and nobody can slip in between. That is what atomic means.
0 rows changed means the condition didn't match, in other words there is no stock. That is how we know who lost the race.

use: A counter or stock held in a single row: put the condition inside the UPDATE.
avoid: Rules spanning several rows or tables (seat, wallet and coupon together): use a lock or a unique constraint.
One very hot row: buyers queue on it, so keep the transaction short.

check.q: Why does `UPDATE ... WHERE stock > 0` not oversell, when SELECT followed by UPDATE does?
check.a: The check and the decrement happen as one step inside the database, so no other buyer can slip in between. If 0 rows change, the stock was already gone.

slides.title: Pressing the elevator button again and again: idempotency tests
slides.tldr: Send the same Idempotency-Key twice: the response is the same and only one charge happens. Send different data with the same key and it must be rejected. That is how you test retries and double clicks.

blocks.title: The elevator button
blocks.body: Press the elevator button five times and one elevator comes, not five. A payment API should behave like that button: the network drops and the client sends the same request again. With the same key, the server recognizes "this is the request I already handled" and returns the earlier response, without charging again.

blocks.caption: On a retry with the same key: the same response, no new charge

actors.label: Client
actors.tip: When the network drops it tries again, with the same key.

actors.label: Payment API
actors.tip: Remembers the key, and doesn't charge again on the second request.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Stores the key and its result.

messages.label: K1 is new: charge, store the result

messages.note: The response got lost on the way, the client doesn't know

messages.label: Yes: here is the earlier result

marks.tip: The HTTP header Idempotency-Key becomes HTTP_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY in the test client (upper case, - turned into _, prefixed with HTTP_).
Counting charges isn't enough; the response must be identical too, or the client gets confused the second time.
On an API with no key handling the second POST charges again, this count is 2, and the test fails.
The same key with a different amount is a client mistake. Quietly returning the earlier result would hide the mistake, so reject it.

blocks.code:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uniq_payment_idempotency_key ON payment (idempotency_key);

-- request A: INSERT (idempotency_key = 'order-42-attempt-1') succeeds, so A charges
-- request B, same instant: the same INSERT fails with a unique violation,
--   so B does not charge; it returns A's stored result, or 409 while A is running

marks.tip: The database lets only one INSERT claim the key. Claim it before charging, and a simultaneous twin cannot charge twice.

blocks.body: Test idempotency by sending twice: the same response, and the effect (the charge) only once.

items: Also send two requests with the same key at the same time (using the Process technique from the earlier slides). Most bugs live here: both see "new key" and charge twice. The UNIQUE index above is what makes one of them lose.

check.q: Why isn't checking only "one charge" enough in an idempotency test?
check.a: The second response must match the first exactly. Otherwise, even with one charge, the client gets a different response and gets confused or tries again.

slides.title: Migration tests: run them on real-looking data
slides.tldr: Go back to the previous version, load old-shaped data (including corner cases), run the migration, then check that the data is intact and that the old code's queries still work.

blocks.body: A migration on an empty test database always passes. In production the trouble is the data: NULLs, duplicates, odd values. Say we add a `mobile` column to `user`. A first draft that makes it NOT NULL fails on any user with no phone, and also breaks the old servers' INSERTs. So the recipe for a migration test is: put real-shaped data in the earlier state, run the migration, then ask two questions. Did the data survive? Does the old code still run?

blocks.caption: Five steps of a migration test

steps.title: 1. Go to the old version
steps.body: Bring the database to the state just before the migration.
steps.tip: Use doctrine:migrations:migrate <previous version>, on a separate test database.

steps.title: 2. Load old data
steps.body: Normal rows, plus NULLs and corner cases.
steps.tip: Whatever you suspect production data contains: empty strings, duplicates, very large values.

steps.title: 3. Run the migration
steps.body: Now migrate to the new version.
steps.tip: If it fails, the error message will tell you which data caused the trouble.

steps.title: 4. Data intact
steps.body: Row counts and values are the same as before.
steps.tip: Lost or changed data is the scariest kind, because it happens silently.

steps.title: 5. Old code works
steps.tip: During a deploy the old servers keep running. If their queries break, some users get errors.

marks.tip: Expand first: old rows and old code keep working because nothing new is required yet.
The tempting version. The corner-case row in the test below makes it fail, which is exactly what the test is for.
NULL, empty and oddly shaped values. If the migration adds NOT NULL or UNIQUE, this is where it breaks.
Imitating the old code: an INSERT without the new column. If this fails, the expand step isn't really backward compatible.

blocks.body: Test migrations on messy, production-like data, not on an empty database.

items: Measure how long the migration takes separately, on staging with production-sized data. Small test data hides both the duration and the locks.
In CI, run "migrate up, then down, then up again" to catch a broken down() early.

check.q: Why does a migration test load old-shaped data first and migrate afterwards? What would be lost if you migrated first and loaded data after?
check.a: The real risk is whether old data (NULLs, duplicates) breaks the migration. If you load data after migrating, that old data is never put to the test.

slides.title: The trap: race tests built on sleep are always green
slides.tldr: A race test that lines things up with sleep() never actually causes the race, so it is always green. Use a start barrier, run it many times rather than once, and use real PostgreSQL.

blocks.body: The easy way to write a race test: launch two processes with a small `usleep` between them. On a fast machine the first finishes before the second even starts, so the race never happens. The test is always green while the bug remains. That makes it the most dangerous kind of test: it gives you a false feeling of safety.

marks.tip: The sleep is a guess. The right timing depends on the machine, the load and PHP warm-up: it works today and fails tomorrow.
Green once means nothing. If one round catches the bug one time in three, 20 rounds miss it only about once in 3,000 runs.
Every round starts from a clean state. Data from the previous round doesn't affect the next.

blocks.title: Three more mistakes that weaken the test
items: Race tests on SQLite: the database's own locking and isolation behave differently
Looking for another process's data inside a transaction-wrapped test: other processes don't see uncommitted data
Looking only at the final result and assuming "it ran once, so it's fine"

aside.body: In race tests, line things up with a signal, not a guess about time. And run them again and again, not once.

items: After fixing the bug, run the test against the old buggy code and watch it fail. You can't trust a test that has never failed.

items.label: Integration tests on a real database

check.q: In a race test, the buggy code still gets a green result. What do you conclude?
check.a: The test is weak: it can't cause the race. Start everyone at the same instant with a barrier, run many rounds, and check that it fails against the buggy code.
